questions.q: In a push-based deployment model, what does the CI pipeline typically need in order to deploy to a production cluster?
options: Nothing beyond write access to the Git repository
Credentials with enough privilege to authenticate directly to the cluster and apply manifests, such as a fetched kubeconfig
A read-only webhook subscription to the cluster's event stream
Access to the cluster's etcd backup snapshots only
questions.explain: Push-based pipelines run commands like `az aks get-credentials` followed by `kubectl apply`, which means the CI system must hold credentials privileged enough to modify the live cluster directly.

questions.q: Why is holding privileged cluster credentials inside a CI system considered a security liability?
options: Because CI systems cannot technically store secrets at all
Because Kubernetes rejects any deployment that originates from outside the cluster network
Because kubeconfig files expire after exactly five minutes in every cloud provider
Because a compromise of the CI system (a leaked secret, a poisoned dependency, a malicious PR) can expose or abuse those same privileged credentials, widening the blast radius
questions.explain: The CI system becomes a high-value target precisely because it has standing, often broadly-scoped, access to production; any compromise of it can be leveraged against the cluster it's authorized to deploy to.

questions.q: What does a pull-based GitOps agent, such as Argo CD or Flux, actually do differently from a push-based pipeline?
options: It still pushes changes from an external pipeline, just using a different credential format
It eliminates the cluster entirely and deploys directly to a CDN
It runs inside the cluster, watches Git using read-only credentials, and applies changes using its own in-cluster RBAC permissions
It requires the cluster's API server to accept more inbound connections than a push-based setup would
questions.explain: A pull-based agent runs in-cluster, authenticates outbound to Git with read-only credentials, and applies changes with permissions scoped by Kubernetes RBAC it already holds — no external system needs a privileged cluster credential.

questions.q: What does the OpenGitOps "Pulled Automatically" principle state?
options: Software agents automatically pull the desired state declarations from the source, rather than an external system pushing them in
All container images must be pulled from a single approved private registry
Developers must manually pull the latest manifests before every deployment
CI pipelines must poll the cluster's API server every five seconds
questions.explain: The Pulled Automatically principle specifically assigns the responsibility of fetching and applying desired state to software agents, not to external CI/CD pipelines pushing changes in.

questions.q: In the pull model described in this lesson, what kind of credential does the GitOps agent use to reach Git, and what does it use to apply changes to the cluster?
options: A cluster-admin kubeconfig to reach Git, and a GitHub personal access token to apply changes
A read-only deploy key or scoped token to reach Git, and its own in-cluster RBAC permissions to apply changes
No credentials of any kind are needed in the pull model
A shared root password used for both Git and the cluster API server
questions.explain: The agent authenticates outbound to Git with read-only credentials and applies manifests using permissions scoped through Kubernetes Roles and RoleBindings it already holds in-cluster — never a privileged external credential.
